title: Minimum wage increase on restaurant employment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy

We will use a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach to estimate the causal effect of the minimum wage increase on restaurant employment. The DID method is appropriate here because we have a treatment group (states with minimum wage increase) and a control group (neighboring states without the increase), and we can compare the changes in employment before and after the policy change.

The key assumption in DID is that, in the absence of the treatment, the treated and control groups would have followed the same trend. This assumption is often referred to as the "parallel trends" assumption.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(plm)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s02_data.csv")

# Convert the data to a panel data structure
pdata <- pdata.frame(data, index = c("unit_id", "period"))

# Estimate the DID model
did_model <- plm(y ~ treat_x_post, data = pdata, model = "within")

# Print the coefficient for the treatment effect
summary(did_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Estimate"]

# Robustness check: Clustered standard errors
coeftest(did_model, vcovHC(did_model, type = "HC1"))
```

## 3. Expected Findings

We expect the coefficient on the `treat_x_post` variable to be negative, indicating that the minimum wage increase led to a reduction in employment at fast-food restaurants in treated states compared to control states. The magnitude of the effect will depend on the data, but we expect it to be economically significant given the size of the minimum wage increase ($2/hr). The parallel trends assumption is crucial for the validity of our DID estimates, and any violations of this assumption could bias our results.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treated=high-wage states, control=neighboring states; shock=minimum wage hike
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Modest employment decline in treated restaurants post minimum wage increase
